title: Value structure — Image Wiki
text:
Value structure
  How light or dark things are, independent of their colour. Squint at any image and what survives is its value structure — and if that does not read, no colour will save it.

  
    Termvalue / lightness structure
    Also calledtonal structure, value massing, notan, lightness
    Not the same asbrightness, saturation, tone, contrast
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The words, kept straightWhy value carries the pictureMassing and keyWhy the subject disappearsCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Squint at any picture, or shrink it to a thumbnail. If what survives still says "a figure in a bright doorway", the image works. If it collapses into grey mush, no amount of colour will rescue it.
That arrangement of light and dark is the value structure, and it is the load-bearing part of nearly every image you will judge.
The words, kept straight
These four terms get used interchangeably and they are not the same.
Lightness is the perceptual axis from black to white. Its formal definition is worth reading slowly: the brightness of an area judged relative to a similarly illuminated area that appears white. A comparison against a white in the same light, not a count of photons — which is why a white shirt in shadow still looks white.
Brightness is how much light you perceive coming from an area, with no reference white involved. That same shirt has high lightness and low brightness at once, and a candle flame in frame has no lightness at all.
Value is the painter's word for the lightness axis, usually on Munsell's 0–10 scale, running upward from black to white.
Tone is the trap. Painters use it for the same axis but often count it from white to black, so "high value" and "high tone" can mean opposite things. If someone says tone, ask which way they count.
Why value carries the picture
Split a picture into a lightness-only layer and a hue-and-chroma-only layer, and only one half is still a picture. David Briggs demonstrates it on Arthur Streeton's Sunlight Sweet, Coogee (SRC-069); here is that split.


Streeton's painting as he painted it
Lightness only — our own luminosity conversion
Hue and chroma only — our own, with lightness flattened


Arthur Streeton, Sunlight Sweet, Coogee, 1890. Public domain. The middle and right panels are ours: the middle keeps each pixel's lightness and throws the colour away, the right keeps hue and chroma exactly as painted and flattens lightness to one value.
The middle panel loses all the colour and loses nothing else. The white path, the dark cliff, the tree mass, the girl in the hat, the crowd on the skyline — every shape you needed is still there, and it would still read at thumbnail size.
The right panel is the one to sit with. Every colour is untouched, and the picture is gone: a soft smear in which the only findable things are the red figure and a few blue-grey patches of sea and shadow, and those only as blobs. You cannot tell there is a path, a cliff or a horizon. Hue and chroma decorate; value draws.


One number worth keeping, because it says what kind of instrument your eye is. Munsell value and CIE L* are spaced so each step looks like an equal jump, which makes them strongly nonlinear against physics: a middle grey (Munsell 5, L* 50) looks halfway between black and white but reflects only about 20% of what a white reflects in the same light. Your eye reports comparisons, not quantities.
Massing and key
Craft practice rather than law: a readable image usually resolves into three or four distinct value masses. Grouping them this way is called massing — Andrew Loomis's value sketches of Howard Pyle's illustrations are this exercise.


The painting as painted, full of gradients and detail
Our own reduction of it to three flat values


Vilhelm Hammershøi, Ida Reading a Letter, 1899. Public domain. The right panel is our own reduction of the left one to three flat greys — no gradients, no modelling, no detail.
Cover the left panel. The right one still says "a woman in black at a white door, a laid table in front of her, a dark floor": three masses, and the composition survives intact. Nothing that was thrown away — the modelling on her sleeve, the grain of the boards, the coffee pot's highlights — was carrying the picture.
The reduction also exposes something the painting hides. Her white apron falls in the same value band as the door behind her, so from the waist down she has no edge at all; only the black bodice separates her from the room. That is a thin margin, and it is the first thing to vanish if someone decides to brighten the shadows.


The lighting is what puts the masses where they are: Light direction decides which planes go dark, Hard and soft light whether the boundaries are edges or gradients, Light falloff how much of the background joins in.
Where the masses sit on the scale is the key: low key in the dark half with small bright accents, high key in the light half with few deep darks.


Low key: everything but the face sits in the dark half
High key: everything but one figure sits in the light half


Rembrandt van Rijn, Self-Portrait, 1659 (National Gallery of Art, Washington). Alfred Sisley, Snow at Louveciennes, 1874. Both public domain.
In the Rembrandt, cap, coat and background all live in the bottom third of the scale, separated by steps so small you have to hunt for the edge between the shoulder and the wall; the face is the only thing allowed up the scale. In the Sisley the opposite: snow, sky and walls fill the top half, and the dark notes are few and small — the woman with the umbrella, the bare trunks, the fence at the bottom left. Your eye goes to the woman rather than to the fence, because she is the dark shape with white on every side of her.
Note what neither picture is. Neither is low in contrast: the Rembrandt runs from near-black to a bright forehead, the Sisley from white snow to those near-black accents. Key describes where the bulk of the picture sits, not how far apart its extremes are.


One warning on the word: painters use key for where the masses sit, while film and CG lighting people use it for how much fill there is. Related, not identical.



James McNeill Whistler, Nocturne: Blue and Silver—Battersea Reach, c. 1870–75. Public domain.
A whole picture made of three masses and almost nothing else: pale sky, mid-value river, near-black barge and foreground. There is no drawing to speak of — the crane and the far chimneys are flat silhouettes, the water has no detail at all — and it still reads as a river at night.
Run the last item on the checklist below on it. The darkest dark is the barge, the nearest thing and the one the composition is arranged around; the lightest light is the far sky. Both are where the picture is about. The few orange specks are worth noticing as the exception: strongly coloured, but barely different in value from the water around them, which is why they read as sparks and not as the subject.


Why the subject disappears
An edge is easiest to see when the two areas differ in value. Two colours that look nothing alike but match in value give the weakest edge there is — Briggs puts it precisely: the grey of equal luminance to a coloured patch is the grey that shows least contrast with it. A mid-red jacket against a mid-green hedge vanishes at thumbnail size.

Structure holdslight wall, mid floor, dark figurethe subject still separatesStructure survives the squintsame three masses, flattenedthe figure is still thereStructure gonefigure now matches the wall

Left is a scene with modelling; middle keeps three flat values and loses nothing that mattered.
Right changes exactly one thing — the figure is now at the wall's value. Everything else is identical and the subject has gone; the only edge left above the floor line is a hairline you have to hunt for. Note what still works there: the floor separates from the wall, because that boundary is still a value boundary.


A second trap sits on top: saturated colours look lighter than a grey of equal luminance — the Helmholtz-Kohlrausch effect — so enjoying the colour skews your reading of its value. Squinting suppresses that glow, which is why it is a technique and not folklore.

Not every black-and-white conversion tells the truth
A colour's value is what survives conversion to greyscale — but only if the conversion is done properly. Photoshop's Desaturate command in RGB mode maps every maximum-chroma colour to the same middle grey, so a fire-engine red and a saturated blue come out identical when they were nothing alike. The same command in Lab mode, or any conversion based on luminosity, gives a result that matches what you see. If you check an image by desaturating it, use a luminosity conversion.

Common mistakes

"Value is just how bright the pixel is." Lightness is judged relative to a white in the same light. A white shirt in shadow keeps a high value even though very little light is coming off it.
"Value and saturation are the same axis." They are independent. See Hue, value and chroma.
"Different colours mean the shapes will separate." Only if the values differ.
"A dark picture is low key." Low key means the masses sit low and the accents are controlled. An underexposed muddle is a muddle.
"Tone and value are interchangeable." Often counted in opposite directions by the people who use them.
"Shading a colour means adding black to it." Black drops chroma faster than value, so the result is too grey for its lightness. Real shading follows the colour down a line of constant saturation — which is why shadows in good paintings still look coloured.


How to check a value structure in five seconds

Squint hard, or shrink the image to a thumbnail. Do the remaining patches still tell you what it is?
Count the value masses. Two to four distinct ones with a clear arrangement usually means a readable image.
Find the subject. Is it a different value from what is directly behind it, or only a different hue?
Locate the lightest light and the darkest dark. Are they near what the image is about? In a photograph the darkest dark is usually a contact shadow (The anatomy of a shadow), so if the deepest black sits in open space, ask why.
Still unsure? Convert to greyscale with a luminosity conversion and look again.
